content: 1. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is strongly recommended for all patients with HIV and drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) who require second-line anti-TB drugs, regardless of their CD4 cell count. This treatment should be initiated as early as possible, ideally within the first eight weeks after starting anti-TB treatment. This recommendation is based on very low-certainty evidence. 2. Routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be provided to all individuals living with HIV who have active TB disease, irrespective of their CD4 cell count. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-certainty evidence. 3. In settings with a high burden of both HIV and TB, ART should be initiated within TB treatment settings. This approach ensures linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART. This recommendation is strong but based on very low-certainty evidence. 4. People living with HIV are approximately 14 times more likely to develop TB disease compared to the general population. They also experience poorer TB treatment outcomes and have more than double the mortality rate during TB treatment compared to all individuals diagnosed with TB. 5. The WHO End TB Strategy, endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2014, provides a strategic framework to achieve TB-related targets within the UN Sustainable Development Goals. This includes ensuring universal health coverage for all individuals affected by TB. 6. Integrated, patient-centered care and prevention of HIV-associated TB are critical components of the End TB Strategy. These interventions aim to prevent TB and address its associated morbidity and mortality through a combination of medical and socioeconomic measures. 7. The importance of integrated, people-centered services was emphasized in the political declarations of the UN high-level meetings on TB and HIV/AIDS. These declarations advocate for collaborative efforts to reduce the burden of HIV-associated TB. 8. WHO first published an interim policy on collaborative TB/HIV activities in 2004, which was updated in 2012. This policy has guided global efforts to address HIV-associated TB, advocating for increased investment and scale-up of collaborative activities. 9. Despite significant progress in collaborative TB/HIV activities and advances in TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, TB remains the leading cause of death among people living with HIV globally. In 2022, TB accounted for 27% of all HIV-related deaths worldwide. 10. Gaps in TB/HIV collaborative activities persist. In 2022, only 64% of new TB cases among people living with HIV were diagnosed and notified. Additionally, the treatment success rate for people with HIV who started TB treatment in 2021 was 79%, lower than the success rate for all TB patients. 11. Since the publication of the 2012 WHO policy on collaborative TB/HIV activities, there have been significant scientific advancements. These include evidence supporting the combined benefits of early ART and TB preventive treatment (TPT), shorter rifamycin-based TPT regimens, and improved diagnostic tools such as C-reactive protein (CRP) testing, chest X-rays with computer-aided detection, and molecular rapid diagnostic tests. 12. WHO has updated its recommendations to reflect these advancements, including the use of shorter TB treatment regimens, earlier initiation of ART after starting TB treatment, and new strategies for HIV testing and care. 13. The updated WHO guidelines aim to reduce suffering and mortality caused by TB and HIV in alignment with global health strategies, including the WHO End TB Strategy and the Global AIDS Strategy. 14. The guidelines are intended for national TB and HIV program managers, healthcare providers, policymakers, and other stakeholders involved in addressing HIV-associated TB. They also serve as a resource for communities, civil society organizations, and individuals at risk of or affected by TB and HIV. 15. WHO emphasizes the importance of integrated, people-centered TB and HIV services. This includes strengthening governance, improving access to quality services, coordinating planning and resource mobilization, and scaling up prevention and treatment efforts. 16. WHO will continue to review and update its recommendations as new evidence becomes available, working closely with member states, technical partners, and funding agencies to ensure effective implementation and communication of updated guidance.
